summary: Defines how to run the WebSocket protocol from RFC 6455 over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection. This lets WebSocket traffic share an HTTP/2 connection with other requests instead of needing its own.

eli5.summary: Rather than building a separate phone line for a chat, this lets the chat share one busy line that already carries many conversations.

questions: how do websockets work over http/2
subtitle: How a WebSocket gets opened on one stream of an HTTP/2 connection, using an extended CONNECT request.

tldr.problem: The WebSocket opening handshake in RFC 6455 relies on the HTTP/1.1 Upgrade mechanism, the Connection and Upgrade header fields and the 101 status code. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams on one connection and has no connection-wide header fields or status codes, so none of that works.
tldr.mechanism: A new SETTINGS parameter lets a server announce support, and an extended CONNECT request carrying a :protocol pseudo-header field set to websocket opens a tunnel on a single HTTP/2 stream. After the handshake, the stream is treated as if it were the TCP connection of RFC 6455.
tldr.outcome: WebSockets and ordinary HTTP/2 traffic can share one TCP connection. The RFC updates RFC 6455 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8441 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 6455.

sections.title: Why WebSockets Need a New Handshake on HTTP/2
sections.content:
RFC 6455 starts a WebSocket by sending an HTTP/1.1 request that uses the Upgrade mechanism to turn a TCP connection from HTTP into a WebSocket connection. That does not carry over to HTTP/2. Because HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams on one connection, it does not allow connection-wide header fields or status codes such as Upgrade, Connection or the 101 (Switching Protocols) response. The RFC 6455 opening handshake requires all of them.

The RFC points out that HTTP offers compatible resource-level semantics across versions but not compatibility at the connection-management level, so protocols that depend on connection details must be updated for each new HTTP version. Bootstrapping from HTTP/2 lets one TCP connection be shared by both protocols and extends HTTP/2's more efficient use of the network to WebSockets.
sections.eli5: The old way of starting a chat was to take over a whole phone line. A shared line carrying lots of calls cannot be taken over, so a new way to start a chat is needed.

sections.title: Announcing Support: The SETTINGS Parameter
sections.content:
The RFC adds a new HTTP/2 SETTINGS parameter named SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL. Its value MUST be 0 or 1. When a client receives the parameter with a value of 1, it MAY use the extended CONNECT when creating new streams. Receipt of the parameter by a server has no effect.

A sender MUST NOT send the parameter with value 0 after previously sending 1, so support cannot be withdrawn once announced.

The opt-in matters because extended CONNECT adds a new pseudo-header field, :protocol, and changes the meaning of :authority. A client that used it without first seeing the setting would hit a peer that treats the request as malformed and answers with a stream error.
sections.eli5: The server puts up a sign saying 'chats are welcome here'. Once the sign is up it can never be taken down, and clients should only start a chat after seeing it.

sections.title: The Extended CONNECT Method
sections.content:
HTTP/2 already has a CONNECT method that tunnels to an external host. The RFC extends it in three ways. A new pseudo-header field :protocol MAY be included on the request HEADERS, naming the protocol to speak on the tunnel; it is single valued and takes a value from the HTTP Upgrade Token Registry. On requests that contain :protocol, the :scheme and :path pseudo-header fields MUST also be included.

Third, on such requests the :authority pseudo-header field is interpreted as for ordinary requests, not as for plain CONNECT. The server MUST NOT create a tunnel to the host named in :authority.

When a server receives a CONNECT request with :protocol, it establishes a tunnel to another service of that protocol type. The service may or may not be co-located with the server.
sections.eli5: A normal CONNECT says 'connect me to that building'. The extended version says 'connect me to the chat service' and lets the server work out where that is.

sections.title: Opening a WebSocket Over One Stream
sections.content:
To start a WebSocket on an HTTP/2 stream, the CONNECT request MUST include :protocol with the value websocket. This request replaces the GET request of RFC 6455 and carries the opening handshake. The scheme MUST be https for wss WebSockets and http for ws WebSockets, and the rest of the target URI is the WebSocket URI.

The Connection and Upgrade header fields MUST NOT be included. Host information travels in :authority. Implementations do not process Sec-WebSocket-Key and Sec-WebSocket-Accept, since :protocol supersedes them. The Origin, Sec-WebSocket-Version, Sec-WebSocket-Protocol and Sec-WebSocket-Extensions fields are used as in RFC 6455, but written in lowercase as HTTP/2 requires.

After a successful handshake the WebSocket is in the OPEN state and the peers carry on with RFC 6455, treating the HTTP/2 stream as the TCP connection. Closure maps over too: an orderly TCP closure becomes the END_STREAM flag, and an abrupt one becomes an RST_STREAM frame with the CANCEL error code.
sections.eli5: The chat is started with a special request instead of the old trick. After that it works just like before, except the shared line plays the part of a private one, and hanging up just closes that one conversation.

sections.title: An Example Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC's example has the server first sending SETTINGS with SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL set to 1. The client then sends a HEADERS frame with :method = CONNECT, :protocol = websocket, :scheme = https, :path = /chat and :authority = server.example.com, plus sec-websocket-protocol offering chat, superchat, sec-websocket-extensions offering permessage-deflate, sec-websocket-version = 13 and an origin.

The server answers with :status = 200 and picks chat as the sub-protocol. After that, both sides exchange WebSocket data in DATA frames, ending with END_STREAM.
sections.eli5: The server says chats are welcome, the client asks for one, the server says yes, and then they talk.

sections.title: Proxies and Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC does not change how WebSockets interact with HTTP forward proxies. A client that reaches a proxy over HTTP/2 should still use a traditional CONNECT, without :protocol, to tunnel to the WebSocket server. The HTTP version running inside that tunnel decides whether WebSockets starts directly or through the extended CONNECT described here.

The RFC also admits that a more native integration with HTTP/2 is possible with larger additions to HTTP/2. This design was chosen to keep complexity low while still solving the main concern of running HTTP/2 and WebSockets at the same time.
sections.eli5: If you go through a go-between, you still ask it the old way. This design is deliberately simple, even though a fancier one could have been built.

sections.title: Security and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
RFC 6455 keeps non-WebSocket clients, especially XMLHttpRequest-based ones, from opening WebSockets, mainly through Sec- prefixed header fields they cannot create. This RFC keeps that protection in two ways. XMLHttpRequest also prohibits the CONNECT method, and a pseudo-header field is connection specific, which HTTP/2 never allows to be created outside the protocol stack.

The security considerations of RFC 6455 Section 10 still apply, except Section 10.8, which is specific to the handshake this document changes.

For IANA, the RFC registers the HTTP/2 setting SETTINGS_ENABLE_CONNECT_PROTOCOL with code 0x8 and initial value 0, and the HTTP upgrade token websocket.
sections.eli5: Ordinary web page scripts cannot send the special request, so they cannot sneak into a chat they should not be in.
